newsitem.title: USA: Genzyme affiliate sees new diabetes therapy.
newsitem.headline: Genzyme affiliate sees new diabetes therapy.

text.p: Genzyme Transgenics Corp reported on Wednesday that it had developed a process that James Geraghty, president and chief executive officer of the company, said "creates a potentially significant and new treatment for diabetes patients."

Genzyme Transgenics said it has "successfully expressed" high levels of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), a protein that is a potential therapy for insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, in the milk of transgenic mice.
"It confirms the ability of transgenic technology to produce a broad and important class of proteins difficult to express in any other system," Geraghty said.
Genzyme Corp owns about 43 percent of the outstanding stock of Genzyme Transgenics.

The production of GAD, a non-secreted protein, "is a significant technical achievement," the company said. It explained that proteins that are not normally secreted by cells are difficult to produce in cell culture because they generally remain within the producing cell.

To generate sufficient quantities of a non-secreted protein, like GAD, the producing cells must be harvested and the protein separated from the cells and other proteins found within those cells, it said.

In transgenic animals, the protein is secreted by the mammary gland cells into the milk of the animal. Genzyme said it has filed for broad patent protection covering the production of non-secreted proteins in milk in the United States.
Mice are used to determine if it is feasible to introduce the human gene in an animal for production of the therapeutic protein, it said.
Goats will be used for commercial production of the therapeutic protein, it added.

In preclinical studies at University of California in Los Angeles and Stanford University, the oral tolerization of the GAD protein suppressed the autoimmune process that leads to the onset of so-called type 1 diabetes in mice, it said.
Genzyme Transgenics has acquired the GAD65 gene from UCLA and is collaborating with Daniel L. Kaufman of UCLA's Molecular Biology Institute on further studies and development for human use.

Type 1 diabetes is characterized by inadequate secretion or utilization of insulin necessary to metabolize carbohydrates. Current treatments are life-long insulin therapy and lifestyle changes involving diet and exercise.
GAD is the second non-secreted protein produced by Genzyme Transgenics. The first, myelin basic protein, is being developed as a potential treatment for multiple sclerosis.
Genzyme Transgenic uses transgenic technology to enable the development and production of recombinant proteins and monoclonal antibodies for medical uses.
